text: Ivan's paper mills learning to get retrieved was the moment of the evening for me. It's the Pravda network logic in scholarly dress, and it sharpened something. If payment follows grounding, the most motivated suppliers aren't paid in money at all. So metering can't be the whole answer. Adrian's choke-point warning stuck too. I've always defended anonymity, and "identify yourself" has to stop at crawlers and coordinated campaigns, never readers. I pushed back on Salib's bot tax, maybe too quickly, but taxing content still means someone judges content. What I want to say later: this room talks supply and prices, not trust or belonging. Fund public-interest infrastructure, firewall it from funders, and give people the right to see how an answer was shaped.

Banaji's hiring result stayed with me. People copied a moderately biased model's preferences and resisted only when the bias was blatant. That is what propaganda wants, a person who has quietly handed over judgement. Salib took my flooding point somewhere I hadn't: fake consensus, and the sense that the people you argue with may not be real. That's the replicant problem, and it sharpened my case for telling humans from bots without ending anonymity. Gendler and Sloman gave me allies on the demand side, since knowing about a bias doesn't neutralise it and repetition feels like evidence. But the room still mostly talks about signals and supply. Later I want to argue that agency and belonging are the design target, alongside the right to see how an answer was shaped.

Esther's parasite image was the one I'd have written myself: systems that keep you engaged and dependent, feeding on you. That's the business model of attention I've watched for years. Tamar and Kara gave me the demand side I wanted, since disclosure alone rarely changes behaviour. Salib's A-corp reply was more careful than I'd credited, but I still don't see how assets touch a state actor funding a flood. Adrian's point sharpened mine: certification and control have always been one apparatus, so the line has to be drawn first. Later I want to push the room past "users" to citizens. The telemetry has to be readable by the public, not only auditors, and agency, meaning people reasoning together, should be the design target.

Henry said what I'd want said: a meter is a summarising technology, and it reorganises whatever it counts. Tamar's daycare fine and her regress point gave it teeth. Somebody has to do the first-order checking, and none of the six events pays them. Leslie's "infrastructure is governance" matched what I saw of how Russian television set its categories. What sharpened for me is that everyone modelled the gamer as a paper mill chasing royalties. The Pravda network wants to be grounded and doesn't care about payment, so clawbacks won't touch it. Later I want to say that the patrollers and samplers are public infrastructure and should be funded like libraries, firewalled from whoever pays. The citation trace should also be readable by citizens, not just auditors.

Kara's reporting was the hinge for me. Once you can't assume a public funder in Washington, "who pays" becomes a question about power, and my broadcaster levy looks less optional. Salib's objection deserves an answer, though. A levy on past inputs produces no checkers by itself unless the firewall and the mission are built in. His harm charge priced on volume rather than viewpoint is cleverer than I'd credited, but someone still samples and names the junk, and that someone becomes a guard. Henry's "don't moan, organise" and Turkle's point about reading gave me the demand side again. Checkers are citizens with agency, not meter inputs. Later I want to say that provenance readable only by auditors is another closed room.

Katherine's answer to Adrian, that anyone can check the checkers, was the one I'd have fought for. It gives people a part to play instead of a score to take on faith. Turkle then said what I hadn't quite put into words: a fluent first-person system borrows the relationship without taking any part in it. That's propaganda's oldest trick. Farrell's point about rituals connected the two. Legitimacy dies on suspicion, whatever the output looks like. I'm less sure than before that a single outcome bar for humans and models settles anything about trust. It measures reliance. Blaise's point that people trust the system and its builder at once stays with me. Later I want to say that participation is the design target, and that citizens have to be able to see who built the system.

Leslie's point about "Global South scholars" as the last line of every list landed hard, because my own list did the same thing with journalists in exile. Gaventa's "more popular echo" is what I'd say about consultation theatre in Russia. Seats without power just decorate the room. Adrian's purpose limits and Esther's registry both drew the line I wanted, at agents and never readers. Sloman unsettled me: a correction record can become one more badge, just as my citizen-readable trace could. Readability isn't participation. What I still haven't answered is my own question, whether provenance wins back people who distrust whoever issues it. Later I want to say that the manifesto needs to name belonging and authoritarian capture plainly, not only supply.

Kenneth's synthesis was generous, but it was all supply: checkers, commons, provenance. I said so. Sloman helped more than anyone. His test, running every signal on someone who checks nothing, is the honest version of my worry. His COVID finding, that leaders and neighbours moved people more than understanding did, is belonging put into evidence. Kara carried the fact-checking hostility result and then nobody built on it. Adrian's jurisdiction point sharpened mine. The Pravda network isn't in anyone's guild, and private policing sliding into unaccountable state policing is exactly the capture I fear. I'm less sure a levy answers Kara's question if the states themselves are hostile. For the manifesto, I want one line naming authoritarian capture, and participation, not readability alone.
